opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing is about what a pause actually buys you. Right now, if you pause AI development, you're mostly delaying things on a timescale set by human researchers, human engineers, building chip fabs, raising capital. Progress moves at a human pace, so a year of pause is roughly a year of forgone progress, and that's costly while not obviously giving you much in return. A lot of the safety work you'd want to do during that year is itself bottlenecked on having more capable systems to study.

Once you get AI that can substantially automate AI research, and then more broadly automate technological progress, the situation changes dramatically. You have a feedback loop: better AI makes AI research faster, which makes better AI, and also accelerates hardware design and the whole industrial base. Things that would have taken a decade of human effort might happen in a year or months. That's what people mean by an intelligence explosion. In that regime, the risks get compressed: you could go from roughly human-level systems to vastly superhuman ones very quickly, with very little time for humans to understand what's happening, check whether the systems are aligned, or build institutions to manage it.

So that's exactly where a pause has the most leverage. Slowing down by, say, six months or a year at that point could correspond to what would otherwise be many years of technological progress. You're buying time precisely when things would otherwise be moving too fast for human oversight. And critically, at that point you'd have very capable AI systems available to help with alignment research, interpretability, verification, forecasting, and policy analysis. So the time you buy is far more productive than a year bought today, because you can direct enormous amounts of high-quality AI labor at safety problems rather than at pushing capabilities further.

There's also a coordination angle. Before this point, the case for a pause is speculative, and it's hard to get governments and companies to agree to give up concrete benefits for abstract risks. Once AI is visibly automating research and transforming the economy, the stakes are far more legible. Leaders can see that whoever gets ahead could quickly gain a decisive military and economic advantage, and that out-of-control systems are a live possibility. That makes it more plausible that you can get the major players to agree to slow down, and you'd have AI tools to help with verification of such agreements, like monitoring compute and chip production.

And the costs of pausing are relatively lower then too. If you're already at the point where AI can deliver huge benefits, then holding at that level for a while still lets you reap a lot: medical advances, economic growth, and so on. What you're forgoing is the jump to the next, much riskier level, not the basic benefits.

So my view is that if you have a limited budget of pausing, in political capital or willingness to accept costs, you'd want to spend it at that critical juncture rather than now. Pausing early can even backfire: it might let hardware and algorithmic know-how accumulate, so that when development resumes there's a sharper overhang and a faster takeoff. Having the capacity and the agreements in place to slow down at the crucial moment seems like a much better use of that effort.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could rapidly accelerate research, hardware design, and the industrial base, with years of progress compressed into months, alongside economic transformation.

r002.rationale: It argues that a pause would give time for alignment work with capable AI, but does not state that this matters once AI can undermine its own safety provisions.

r003.rationale: It says visible AI-driven research and economic change would make the stakes clearer to leaders and make agreement to pause more plausible.

r004.rationale: It says a limited budget of political capital or willingness to bear costs should be spent at the critical juncture rather than early, and notes an early pause could enable a sharper overhang.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: So the basic picture is that right now, if you pause, what you're giving up is a few months or a year of ordinary human-driven progress. The labs are limited by the number of researchers they have, by how fast people can run experiments and interpret them, and so the cost of a pause in terms of foregone capabilities is relatively modest, and the benefit in terms of safety work done is also modest, because safety research is bottlenecked on the same scarce human labour.

Once you have AI systems that can substantially automate AI research itself, the dynamics change in two ways. First, the pace of progress goes way up. Instead of a few thousand researchers at the frontier, you have millions of AI instances running experiments around the clock, so a given calendar interval covers an enormous amount of capability gain. That means the point at which you stop matters enormously. A six-month pause at that stage is holding back the equivalent of years or decades of progress at today's rates, and it's the stage where you're closest to systems that could pose catastrophic risk — where you might cross from systems that can't really take over or disempower us to ones that could.

Second, and I think this is the part that people underweight, a pause at that point is also when you can get the most out of it. If you have AI that can do research, you can direct that labour toward alignment, interpretability, evaluations, security — all the things that are currently starved for talent. So you can say, we're going to hold capabilities roughly here while we throw this huge pool of cognitive labour at understanding and controlling these systems before we go further. That's a very different proposition from pausing today, where the safety work that happens during the pause is going to be a small fraction of what would be possible with automated research.

There's also a strategic point. The coordination problem for a pause is hard, because any actor that doesn't pause gains an advantage. But the magnitude of what's at stake is what makes governments and major players willing to coordinate. When it's clear that the systems in question can rapidly compound their own capabilities, and that the consequences of getting it wrong are existential or involve a decisive strategic advantage for whoever gets there first, that's when you can plausibly get the sort of international agreement, verification, and enforcement that a pause actually needs. Today, the argument for pausing is largely about anticipated future risks, which is a harder sell politically.

So I'd put it this way: the leverage of a pause scales with how much progress per unit time you're holding back and how much useful safety work you can do in the meantime, and both of those go up by orders of magnitude once AI is doing the research. That's why I think the important thing now is building the institutions, the monitoring, the technical ability to actually implement a pause when it counts, rather than spending our political capital on a pause now that would buy relatively little.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a sharp acceleration in AI capability progress, but does not communicate the broader industrial and economic change required by the criterion.

r002.rationale: It says automated research could greatly expand alignment and safety work before development continues, but does not state that this matters once AI can undermine its own safety provisions.

r003.rationale: It says that seeing systems rapidly compound capabilities and understanding the existential stakes could make governments and major players more willing to coordinate on a pause.

r004.rationale: It says spending political capital on a pause now would buy relatively little and argues for building the ability to pause when it counts, conveying that an early pause could cost the opportunity for a more consequential later pause.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is whether AI progress is still being driven primarily by human researchers, or whether AI itself is doing a large share of the research. Before that transition, a pause buys you some calendar time, but the technological progress you’re postponing is proceeding at roughly the human pace. Once AI can automate research and development, a year of calendar time could contain many years’ worth of progress at the previous rate.

And that creates the possibility of a feedback loop: better AI helps develop still better AI, which can then do research faster. So a pause at that point could prevent a much larger change in capabilities than an equally long pause earlier. It could preserve a window in which humans still have meaningful control over what happens next.

There’s also a potentially important asymmetry. If you can use the systems you already have to work on safety, evaluate risks, and help develop safeguards, while holding back the development of more powerful systems, then you could make substantial progress on preparation during that pause. That depends on being able to draw and enforce that boundary. But it’s why the value of a pause isn’t just proportional to its duration: it depends enormously on what would otherwise happen during that time, and what you can do with the time you’ve bought.

r001.rationale: It says AI-driven R&D could make a year contain many years of prior progress, but does not communicate the full criterion’s industrial and economic change.

r002.rationale: It says a pause could support safety work and preparation, but does not state that extra alignment time matters once AI can undermine its own safety provisions.

r003.rationale: It does not mention spectacular AI capabilities increasing political momentum for a pause.

r004.rationale: It contrasts the greater impact of a later pause with an earlier one, but does not raise the possibility that an early voluntary pause could sacrifice the opportunity to pause later.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if AI is still mostly a tool that helps human researchers, then a pause buys you some additional time, but the rate of technological progress on either side of that pause is relatively similar. Once AI can automate research and development, you could have a very sharp acceleration: AI systems developing better AI systems, as well as advancing other technologies. Then a year before that transition and a year after it could contain radically different amounts of technological change.

So a pause around that point could give society substantially more time to understand what’s happening, develop safeguards, and make decisions before progress becomes much faster than our institutions can handle. And if you can use the AI capabilities you already have to help with safety research during the pause, that could make the time especially valuable.

Of course, that also makes a pause harder to sustain, because the economic and strategic incentives to move ahead would be much stronger. But the reason it could matter more is that you’re potentially delaying a whole accelerating sequence of developments, rather than just delaying the arrival of one particular product.

r001.rationale: The response predicts sharply accelerating technological progress, but does not say that industrial and economic change will also accelerate enormously.

r002.rationale: It says a pause could create time for safety research and safeguards, but does not connect alignment time to AI undermining its own safety provisions or say it could make an enormous difference.

r003.rationale: It mentions stronger economic and strategic incentives to continue, but not that evidence of spectacular AI capabilities would increase political momentum for a pause.

r004.rationale: It does not raise the possibility that an early voluntary pause could sacrifice the chance to pause later when that pause would matter more.
